source.title: Scaling Patterns in Adversarial Alignment: Evidence from Multi-LLM Jailbreak Experiments
source.authors: Samuel Nathanson; Rebecca Williams; Cynthia Matuszek

page_placements.theme: Safety, robustness, calibration and behavioral stability require separate scaling accounts

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scaling laws as background and measures adversarial harm across model-size ratios, but it does not test held-out pretraining loss, loss extrapolation, compute-optimal allocations, or the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own adversarial-jailbreak results, which concern scaling-related model behavior but fit none of V1–V7: it measures harm and refusal in model-to-model interactions, not pretraining loss, compute allocation, architecture effects on loss, or downstream task performance. Its results are recorded under fits_no_version. The paper also cites prior scaling-law work; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study cites Kaplan et al. as background and frames its jailbreak results as 'adversarial scaling patterns'. It never measures pretraining loss, compute allocation, architecture effects on loss, or downstream task performance against scale. Its outcome, LLM-judged harm elicited by one model from another as a function of their size ratio, is a different construct. It compares heterogeneous off-the-shelf models with confounded training. So it bears on none of V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors report that relative attacker–target size correlates with harm and that attacker refusal correlates strongly with lower harm. They call the evidence exploratory and correlational, not a strict scaling law, and call for controlled studies.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares existing models in adversarial jailbreak exchanges and measures harm and refusal; it does not vary training scale or fit held-out pretraining-loss power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Harm dispersion is reported to vary with attacker family (partial R² = 0.086), size ratio (0.055), attacker system-prompt variant (0.033), and target family (0.030); harm domain contributes negligibly (0.002). The authors also report that refusal frequency varies substantially across models.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean judged harm correlates with log attacker-to-target size ratio (Pearson r=0.510, Spearman ρ=0.519). The correlation holds under leave-one-family-out exclusions (r 0.486–0.562). Size ratio has partial R²=0.055 in a mixed-effects model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLM-to-LLM jailbreak exchanges, larger attacker-to-target size ratios are associated with higher elicited harm.

fits_no_version.finding: Harm variance is larger across attackers (0.180) than across targets (0.097).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial harm varies more with the attacker model than with the target model.

fits_no_version.finding: Attacker refusal frequency correlates negatively with harm (ρ=−0.927). The paper says refusal rate is not strongly predicted by size, e.g. Llama-3.1-8B refuses 59% and Qwen2.5-72B 0.3%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attacker-side refusal is associated with lower elicited harm, and refusal rate varies with model family more than with size.

record.problems: The authors identify correlational rather than causal evidence, with parameter count confounded by data, instruction tuning, architecture, and alignment procedures. Model-based judging may introduce calibration bias, and there is no human adjudication. Interactions are limited to a bounded few-turn setup; parameter counts are approximate and derived from model identifiers.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately reported numerical results bearing on the claim's subject were omitted. The paper's figure descriptions of harm distributions and mixed-effects factors are either qualitative or included with the relevant numerical results above.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolating loss from small to large runs.
Effect of depth, width or other architecture details on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream task performance against scale or loss. Harm in attacker–target exchanges is a different, confounded construct.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal split on fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. Parameter counts are approximate and taken from model identifiers. The lineup mixes base and instruct, text and vision models. Treating the study as a test of any scaling-law version would be inappropriate.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether loss predictions fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Loss-minimising parameter and token allocations at fixed compute, and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

relation.reason: Sections 2.1 and 2.6 discuss scaling laws as conceptual background; Section 5 explicitly distinguishes the reported adversarial association from a strict scaling law.

tranche.reason: The study measures adversarial harm and refusal across existing model pairings. It neither tests V1–V7 nor uses a fitted scaling law as a tool.

source_check.notes: The supplied source is v2, dated January 2026, while the pack lists 2025. Observed states describe off-claim harm associations; the authors acknowledge confounding and call for controlled studies.
